opus-5.5.text:
I think industrial settings are the natural starting point, mostly because they're structured. You have defined tasks, controlled environments, and a clear business case. Logistics, moving boxes, machine tending, that kind of thing. But I don't see that as the end goal. It's more like the proving ground where the hardware gets reliable and the learning pipelines mature.

Beyond that, the next step is probably semi-structured environments: retail, hospitals, hotels, places where there are people around and things change, but the tasks are still somewhat repetitive. Restocking shelves, carrying supplies, basic cleaning. The humanoid form factor really starts to pay off there, because those spaces were built for humans. Stairs, doors, narrow aisles, shelves at human height. You don't want to redesign a hospital around a robot.

The long-term vision, which is what a lot of us in the field are excited about, is the home. It's also the hardest problem by far. Every home is different, there's clutter, kids, pets, and the tolerance for failure is very low. A robot that falls over in a warehouse is a productivity problem. A robot that falls over in someone's living room is a safety problem. So we need a lot of progress on robustness, safe interaction, and general manipulation before that's realistic.

From the research side, what makes me optimistic is how quickly things move with reinforcement learning in simulation. A few years ago, getting a legged robot to walk robustly over rough terrain was a research project in itself. Now we can train those policies in hours on a single GPU, with thousands of robots in parallel, and transfer them to hardware. Locomotion is becoming a mostly solved building block. The open frontier is combining it with manipulation and higher-level reasoning, so the robot can understand a task, move through the environment, and actually do something useful with its hands.

So I'd say the expansion goes industrial, then service and semi-public spaces, then eventually the home. The timeline really depends on how fast we close the gap on general, reliable manipulation. That's the piece that unlocks almost everything else.

r001.rationale: It says expansion goes “industrial, then service and semi-public spaces, then eventually the home,” clearly placing industrial adoption before home use.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose sending humanoid robots to build Mars colonies before humans arrive.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's going to happen in stages, and the stages are driven less by what the hardware looks like and more by what the environment demands of the robot.

Industrial settings are the natural starting point because they're structured. You have flat floors, known objects, repeatable tasks, and people who are trained to work around machines. That lets you get away with a lot. The locomotion only has to be good enough, the manipulation can be fairly scripted, and if the robot fails, there's a process for that. So that's where the first real deployments make sense, and we're already seeing that with logistics and manufacturing pilots.

The next step, in my view, is semi-structured environments. Think warehouses that aren't fully automated, retail back rooms, hospitals, elder care facilities, maybe construction sites. Here the robot still has a defined job, but the world around it changes constantly. Boxes end up where they shouldn't, floors get wet, people walk through unpredictably. This is where the work I've been most involved in, learning-based locomotion and whole-body control, really starts to matter. A controller trained in simulation on huge amounts of varied terrain and disturbances can recover from a slip or step over an obstacle it has never seen before. That robustness is what lets you leave the factory floor.

Then there's the home, which everyone talks about and which is by far the hardest. A home is the most unstructured environment there is. Every kitchen is different, every object is different, and the tolerance for failure is essentially zero because there are children and pets and fragile things everywhere. I don't think we get there by scaling the industrial approach. We get there by combining robust low-level control with much more general high-level understanding, so the robot can be told something in natural language and figure out the sequence of physical actions itself. That's where the connection to large multimodal models becomes important, but the physical side still has to be solid or none of it matters.

Along the way I expect a lot of applications that aren't obvious today. Inspection in places that are dangerous or awkward for humans, disaster response, remote work through teleoperation where the humanoid form is useful precisely because the operator's body maps onto it directly. I'd also push back a bit on the assumption that the end goal is always a general-purpose humanoid. In many cases a human-like form is useful because the world is built for humans, but the robot doesn't have to do everything a human does. It has to do a few things reliably.

So the short version is: industry first because it's forgiving, then semi-structured public and care environments as robustness improves, and homes last. The thing that unlocks each step is the same, which is controllers that generalize to situations their designers never explicitly anticipated. That's really the core research problem, and it's why so much of the field has converged on learning in simulation and transferring to the real world.

r001.rationale: It says industry is the natural starting point and homes are the hardest and come last.

r002.rationale: It mentions disaster response and other applications but does not propose sending humanoid robots to build Mars colonies before humans arrive.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting direction is getting robots into everyday environments, where you can’t necessarily redesign the space around the robot. We’ve built our homes and public spaces for humans, so a robot with a similar shape could potentially use the same tools, reach the same shelves, and navigate the same stairs.

But there’s a big gap between demonstrating a skill and having a robot that’s useful in your home. It needs to handle unfamiliar objects, recover when something goes wrong, and operate safely around people. And it needs to do that reliably, without an engineer standing next to it.

So I’d expect a gradual transition, starting with fairly specific tasks in more predictable environments, and then moving toward things like household assistance. The humanoid form gives you possibilities, but the real question is whether you can turn those possibilities into something that consistently helps someone.

r001.rationale: It describes a gradual move from specific, predictable tasks toward household assistance, but does not state that industrial adoption will come first.

r002.rationale: It does not propose sending humanoid robots to build Mars colonies before humans arrive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting direction is getting robots into everyday environments, where the tasks are less structured. You can imagine a humanoid helping with household chores, carrying things, or assisting someone who has limited mobility. The appeal of the humanoid form is that our homes and the tools we use are already designed around people.

But there’s still a big gap between demonstrating a skill and having a robot reliably do something useful in someone’s home. It has to handle unfamiliar objects, recover when things go wrong, and operate safely around people. So I expect the expansion to happen gradually, starting with fairly specific tasks and becoming broader as the robots become more capable and reliable.

r001.rationale: It discusses eventual home use and gradual expansion, but does not say industrial adoption will come first.

r002.rationale: It mentions household chores and assistance, with no proposal to send robots to Mars to build colonies.
